nameStory: The chameleon shrimp gets its name from its remarkable ability to change colors to match its surroundings, just like the famous color-changing lizards. This tiny crustacean can shift from translucent to brown, green, or reddish hues depending on the background where it's swimming. It's nature's own little master of disguise in the shallow waters!
description: The chameleon shrimp is a small, translucent crustacean that looks like a tiny glass shrimp with a noticeably curved or bent body shape. Growing up to about an inch long (26mm), it has a delicate, almost ethereal appearance as it darts through shallow coastal waters. Despite its name, it's not actually a true shrimp but belongs to a group called opossum shrimp or mysid shrimp. Originally from European waters, this little immigrant made its way to North American coasts in the mid-20th century.

idTips.label: Distinctly bent body
idTips.description: The body has a pronounced curved or kinked appearance, like a tiny translucent banana, which is immediately noticeable when viewed from the side

idTips.label: Color-changing ability
idTips.description: Watch for subtle color shifts from clear to brownish, greenish, or reddish tints as it moves over different backgrounds - the change happens gradually over several minutes

idTips.label: Swimming behavior
idTips.description: Swims with quick, jerky movements punctuated by brief gliding periods, often in small groups near the water's surface or among vegetation

idTips.label: Translucent appearance
idTips.description: Body is largely see-through like frosted glass, allowing you to glimpse internal structures and making it blend seamlessly with the water

idTips.label: Size and proportions
idTips.description: About the length of your thumbnail with a relatively robust middle section that tapers toward both ends, giving it a football-like profile when viewed from above

habitat: Look for chameleon shrimp in shallow coastal waters throughout New England, especially in protected bays, tidal pools, salt marshes, and areas where fresh water meets salt water. They're remarkably adaptable to different salt levels, so you might spot them in brackish estuaries as well as fully marine environments. They prefer areas with some vegetation or structure to hide among, often swimming just below the surface or near the bottom in depths of just a few feet.

seasonality.spring: Most active as waters warm, often seen in large numbers in shallow areas. This is prime time for spotting their color-changing abilities as they move between different substrates.
seasonality.summer: Peak abundance and activity, easily observed during the day in tide pools and shallow bays. Their translucent bodies catch the sunlight beautifully.
seasonality.fall: Still active but beginning to move to slightly deeper waters. Numbers may seem reduced in the shallowest areas where they're easiest to spot.
seasonality.winter: Much less visible as they retreat to deeper, warmer waters or become less active. Rarely seen in typical shallow-water observation spots.

funFact: Chameleon shrimp are actually carrying their babies around with them - females have a special pouch (like a kangaroo!) where they keep their developing young, which is why they're called 'opossum shrimp' despite being neither opossums nor true shrimp!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with small glass shrimp or other mysid species, but the chameleon shrimp's distinctly kinked body shape is the key difference - think of it as the 'hunchbacked' mysid. Memory trick: 'Chameleon has character' - both the color-changing ability and that characteristic curved posture make it stand out.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called a 'shrimp,' chameleon shrimp belong to a completely different group of crustaceans called mysids or opossum shrimp. True shrimp have different body structures and lack the distinctive brood pouch that gives opossum shrimp their marsupial nickname.
compareHints: Since there are no other Praunus species in New England waters, compare the chameleon shrimp to other mysids by looking for that signature bent body shape. Other mysid species in the region tend to have straighter, more torpedo-shaped bodies and may not show the same dramatic color-changing abilities. The curved posture is really your best field mark for distinguishing chameleon shrimp from its mysid cousins.
